<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-0e7822ea0cb4f1b1">Why does state-aware fusion vary across examples?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aadaf2m2">AdaF²M²: Comprehensive Learning and Responsive Leveraging Features in Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Activity and feedback change which signals are trustworthy. The adapter weights complementary masks per state; one fusion coefficient is not permanent importance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Behavioral history can dominate for an established user and content for a new one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:adaf2m2" data-paper-title="AdaF²M²: Comprehensive Learning and Responsive Leveraging Features in Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c63df32fe423b84d">How do AdaF²M² multiple masked forwards differ from dropping features once?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aadaf2m2">AdaF²M²: Comprehensive Learning and Responsive Leveraging Features in Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Several masks retain complementary views. A state-aware adapter combines them by user/item reliability; one perturbed output or uniform averaging does not implement this.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Combine behavior-masked and content-masked views differently for new and mature items.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15816">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2501.15816-adaf2m2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c63df32fe423b84d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:adaf2m2" data-paper-title="AdaF²M²: Comprehensive Learning and Responsive Leveraging Features in Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7d8fa2ddf0c300e8">How does multi-forward fusion differ from feature dropout?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aadaf2m2">AdaF²M²: Comprehensive Learning and Responsive Leveraging Features in Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Single dropout trains robustness to missing inputs. Multi-forward retains alternatives and learns state-specific fusion, adding execution cost even at equal parameter count.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Keeping price-present and price-absent predictions for fusion differs from randomly deleting price once.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15816">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2501.15816-adaf2m2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7d8fa2ddf0c300e8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:adaf2m2" data-paper-title="AdaF²M²: Comprehensive Learning and Responsive Leveraging Features in Recommendation System" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae32381c26ab8834">Which axis should AdaF²M² softmax normalize?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aadaf2m2">AdaF²M²: Comprehensive Learning and Responsive Leveraging Features in Recommendation System</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalize branches separately for each example, with compatible representation widths. Do not couple different users through a batch-level softmax.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two users with three views each need two independent three-weight sums.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15816">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2501.15816-adaf2m2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae32381c26ab8834">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:argus" data-paper-title="Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-argus-3c7d662d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-06db608db356f93c">How read ARGUS&#x27;s feedback–item joint distribution?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aargus">Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Predict feedback from history, then condition item probability on it and multiply. True feedback is training supervision, not an inference input unless specified externally under protocol.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Likes can favor relatable clips while long watches favor tutorials.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15994-argus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-06db608db356f93c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:argus" data-paper-title="Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-34e00691c873ae6a">How does feedback-then-item differ from direct next-item prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aargus">Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>ARGUS factors joint action into feedback type then conditional item, sharing a trunk while preserving feedback distinctions. Inference cannot read future feedback. Local module ablation is negative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Expected long watch and quick skip can favor different items for the same history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15994-argus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-34e00691c873ae6a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:argus" data-paper-title="Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e31c2f745c08191d">How does conditional factorization differ from a parallel auxiliary head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aargus">Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A parallel head adds loss without necessarily changing item prediction. ARGUS explicitly conditions items on feedback, so feedback errors can propagate. Measure both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Separate “will like” and item outputs are multitask, not a feedback-conditioned generator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15994-argus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e31c2f745c08191d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:argus" data-paper-title="Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a3a287cea14c8c52">Why distinguish DIN and next-item-only baselines?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aargus">Scaling Recommender Transformers to One Billion Parameters</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Yandex</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>DIN compares whole models; matched next-item-only isolates feedback factorization. Both local comparisons lack gains, and neither should hide the other&#x27;s negative evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Overall proximity to DIN can coexist with degradation after adding the feedback path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15994">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15994-argus/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a3a287cea14c8c52">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bst" data-paper-title="Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-bst-730383cc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a525ddf7b84c2c8a">Why include BST&#x27;s candidate token in history encoding rather than concatenating it only in the final MLP?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abst">Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Attention with the candidate lets history representations adapt early and learns both behavior-to-behavior and target-to-history relations. Late concatenation only interacts with an already compressed representation. The result is candidate-conditioned, not universal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Hiking shoes can amplify a related camping and hiking history, while a camera should refocus the encoding on photography.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06874">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1905.06874-bst/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a525ddf7b84c2c8a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bst" data-paper-title="Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a856ffcdedab0d96">How does BST jointly attending over a candidate and history differ from DIN using a candidate to weight history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abst">Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>DIN mainly learns candidate-to-action activation. BST also enables interactions among past actions and embeds the candidate jointly, allowing context to change an action&#x27;s meaning. This costs more sequence computation and can limit reuse across candidates; compare matched budgets and history windows.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A camera click might be incidental, but later lens and tutorial views reinforce photography intent. A different candidate can change this jointly encoded state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06874">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1905.06874-bst/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a856ffcdedab0d96">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bst" data-paper-title="Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-54c96f178108af99">What does BST&#x27;s self-attention add over fixed history pooling, and at what cost?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abst">Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed pooling uses predetermined or simplified action weights and can miss combinations. BST learns pairwise contextual dependencies, with sequence-length-related computation and possible re-encoding for each candidate. Flexibility alone is not a win; compare matching data, budgets, and candidate protocols.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A camera view followed by a lens view can reflect a different purchase stage than a camera view alone. Attention can combine them but costs more with thousands of events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06874">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1905.06874-bst/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-54c96f178108af99">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:bst" data-paper-title="Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-f764ff81a314536c">Why not cache BST&#x27;s candidate-conditioned state as a user embedding shared by all candidates?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abst">Behavior Sequence Transformer for E-commerce Recommendation in Alibaba</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A candidate participating in self-attention can write into hidden history states; substituting it changes downstream inputs. Without an isolation mask, caching is valid only for the specific dependency conditions. The local candidate-aware Transformer versus DIN is not a demonstration of shared user-side caching.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A state computed for shoes can emphasize shoe history and bias a movie score. A shared cache must stop before candidate information is written.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06874">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1905.06874-bst/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f764ff81a314536c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cadet" data-paper-title="CADET: Context-Conditioned Ads CTR Prediction With a Decoder-Only Transformer" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-cadet-4647b60d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-b40ffc952504d31e">Why does CADET emphasize when post-scoring context becomes visible?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acadet">CADET: Context-Conditioned Ads CTR Prediction With a Decoder-Only Transformer</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Training logs may include information created only after scoring. Using it before scoring misaligns training and serving. Encode cacheable history first, then introduce context only at its legitimate stage; timing is part of the feature contract.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A user&#x27;s reaction after an impression can enter the next history, but cannot predict the current click before that impression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11410">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.11410-cadet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b40ffc952504d31e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cadet" data-paper-title="CADET: Context-Conditioned Ads CTR Prediction With a Decoder-Only Transformer" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3572deb35e23e95e">Why does CADET put cacheable history and post-scoring context in different information-flow stages?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acadet">CADET: Context-Conditioned Ads CTR Prediction With a Decoder-Only Transformer</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The cache must remain valid when candidates or later context change. CADET encodes history and scores candidates before injecting post-scoring context at the allowed stage, preventing use of information unavailable at serving time. Mixing everything from the start can invalidate reuse and create training-serving mismatch despite better offline scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not write ad A&#x27;s post-scoring context into shared history before evaluating ad B. Keep the shared prefix distinct from later conditional state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11410">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.11410-cadet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3572deb35e23e95e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cadet" data-paper-title="CADET: Context-Conditioned Ads CTR Prediction With a Decoder-Only Transformer" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4ea6effe523c3e05">How does staged context in CADET differ from feeding all log fields into a Transformer together?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acadet">CADET: Context-Conditioned Ads CTR Prediction With a Decoder-Only Transformer</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Indiscriminate concatenation can expose unavailable fields and leak candidate computations into shared history. Separating cacheable state from post-scoring context limits arbitrary interactions but preserves serving consistency. Local public-data proxies do not verify the full timing of production advertising features.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Mixing current-request features with the next action in one sequence invites a shortcut; stage boundaries allow only evidence available when the request arrives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11410">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.11410-cadet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4ea6effe523c3e05">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cadet" data-paper-title="CADET: Context-Conditioned Ads CTR Prediction With a Decoder-Only Transformer" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-e6af216519561e37">When does new CADET context invalidate cached history K/V?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acadet">CADET: Context-Conditioned Ads CTR Prediction With a Decoder-Only Transformer</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · LinkedIn</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Check whether it changes history inputs, masks, or model parameters. The shared K/V stays valid only if context enters a later candidate-query path. The source formula lets a context query read prior history; it does not authorize feeding arbitrary context back into the cached backbone. Inspect actual tensor dependencies.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A change to the query can reuse the history K/V; changing history time encodings requires recomputation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11410">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.11410-cadet/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e6af216519561e37">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ccformer" data-paper-title="CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-ccformer-b04b720c" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9e54784b884cf046">Why project CCFormer fields separately instead of treating IDs, content, and history as homogeneous tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Accformer">CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent Platform and Content Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different sources and scales benefit from their own projections, followed by cross-attention, which limits dominance by a strong field. Hierarchical compression separately controls history cost. This jointly addresses feature interaction and sequence length, not simply Transformer depth.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A user ID is a sparse lookup and content represents semantics. Separate projections preserve both before interaction instead of favoring frequent IDs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28070">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.28070-ccformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9e54784b884cf046">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ccformer" data-paper-title="CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-16b5de07814be92e">Why does CCFormer expand compression receptive fields for distant history while retaining recent detail?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Accformer">CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent Platform and Content Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Old sequences are large, and per-event interactions can consume ranking budget. Recent behavior can signal changing intent and lose detail if merged early. CCFormer hierarchically mixes old tokens while keeping field-specific projections and cross-attention. Sequence shortening and field interaction solve different problems, so length alone cannot measure effectiveness.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Merge many similar views from last month but preserve today&#x27;s views of two different sizes; candidate fields can still query compressed long-term interests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28070">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.28070-ccformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-16b5de07814be92e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ccformer" data-paper-title="CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-021f89a6ded28d16">What do CCFormer&#x27;s progressive compression and fixed last-N truncation each lose?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Accformer">CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent Platform and Content Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Truncation removes distant events entirely; compression retains coarse older signals at less cost but can erase rare details. Keeping recent resolution while broadening old receptive fields is not lossless. A local GRU comparison does not establish a ranking of all long-sequence methods.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Compression can retain last year&#x27;s photography interest and three recent camping actions but forget one camera model. Last-ten truncation may forget photography entirely.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28070">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.28070-ccformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-021f89a6ded28d16">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ccformer" data-paper-title="CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7f9b2732273cf149">How does hierarchical token mixing in CCFormer differ from compressing the whole sequence uniformly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Accformer">CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent Platform and Content Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Expand the old-history receptive field by layer and temporal region, keep the recent fine-grained path, and use field-specific query projections for interactions. Uniform merging loses temporal resolution allocation. For the small local core, verify connectivity and length changes rather than just runnable tensor shapes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The first layer can keep four recent actions as individual tokens and merge eight older ones. A later layer expands the old window without averaging away a just-recorded key click.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28070">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.28070-ccformer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7f9b2732273cf149">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:chronicle-rec" data-paper-title="ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-chronicle-rec-efcf1d9a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae60800a02e46d24">Why does ChronicleRec represent near, middle, and distant history instead of a few unordered interest tokens?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Achronicle-rec">ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multi-scale pooling preserves temporal structure. Query anchors delimit the past being summarized so stable preferences and recent changes remain distinct. Candidate-independent Chronicle Tokens can be cached, but public compression can still discard target-specific details.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A long-term science-fiction preference and this week&#x27;s parenting interest mean more with time scales than as two unordered keywords.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.12375-chronicle-rec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae60800a02e46d24">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:chronicle-rec" data-paper-title="ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fe7e940e49d3f624">Why must a Chronicle Token have a time anchor and summarize only preceding events?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Achronicle-rec">ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Without the boundary, an earlier representation could include future events, violating temporal causality and making cache meaning unclear. ChronicleRec compresses different ranges, anchors queries on the timeline, reads earlier events only, and masks recent behavior in multiple ways to align short-term intent. Anchored candidate-independent summaries are reusable across candidates.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A Wednesday summary must not include Friday&#x27;s camera purchase when scoring Thursday lens recommendations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.12375-chronicle-rec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fe7e940e49d3f624">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:chronicle-rec" data-paper-title="ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-491ae24f291ae309">How does ChronicleRec alignment pretraining differ from ordinary next-item prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Achronicle-rec">ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Branches hide different lengths of recent actions so compressed older history must predict recent intent without nearby evidence. Ordinary next-item prediction may lean on adjacent actions. Do not return hidden targets to evaluation inputs, or the compression test loses its meaning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Hide the latest three parenting views and predict the new interest from older history instead of guessing the next item from the last parenting item.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.12375-chronicle-rec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-491ae24f291ae309">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:chronicle-rec" data-paper-title="ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae7ea3a33cae636b">Why normalize Chronicle Token pooling by valid mask count and read at the query position?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Achronicle-rec">ChronicleRec: Pre-training Temporally Anchored Tokens for Lifelong User Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Padding should not shrink short histories; masks and a safe denominator average real events only. Read after causal encoding at the query anchor so the state summarizes only earlier events. Other positions and padded events can alter semantics without causing shape errors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A four-slot window with two real actions divides by two. Put the query after both to summarize both; a query between them cannot see the later one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12375">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.12375-chronicle-rec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae7ea3a33cae636b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:clockrope" data-paper-title="ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-clockrope-0d0da402" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-a12f3605b45b2935">Why use a periodic kernel in ClockRoPE rather than assuming relevance always decays with distance?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclockrope">ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · YouTube / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Habits may repeat by hour or weekday. The periodic kernel restores similarity at specific offsets through its rotary frequencies. It is a prior, and proxies without real timestamps are not evidence of periodic behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A Friday film habit makes a seven-day gap informative; for an irregular viewer the same periodic bonus can add noise.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26369">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.26369-clockrope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a12f3605b45b2935">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:clockrope" data-paper-title="ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4dacd6aabb5cf7c7">Why can ClockRoPE give higher relevance to a one-week gap than to a two-day gap?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclockrope">ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · YouTube / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Behavior may recur periodically rather than decay monotonically. ClockRoPE samples rotary frequencies from the desired periodic kernel&#x27;s spectrum so query-key dot products strengthen again at matching times of day or week. Ordinary RoPE can share channels to retain recency. Periodicity is a bias, not a universal user habit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Last Monday morning commute news can be more relevant to this Monday than Saturday-night entertainment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26369">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.26369-clockrope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4dacd6aabb5cf7c7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:clockrope" data-paper-title="ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5181ac128751cc15">How does ClockRoPE differ from adding a weekday feature?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclockrope">ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · YouTube / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A weekday feature is an absolute time label. ClockRoPE changes pairwise attention directly through relative query-key rotations and a periodic similarity kernel. They may overlap or complement one another; the mechanism alone does not guarantee better results.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A Friday label says what day it is; rotation directly relates this Friday to last Friday in attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26369">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.26369-clockrope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5181ac128751cc15">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:clockrope" data-paper-title="ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-45fd047e4127727e">Why must ClockRoPE&#x27;s day and week periods match the timestamp unit?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclockrope">ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · YouTube / Google DeepMind</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The local kernel uses periods 24 and 168 when gaps are in hours. Raw seconds shift phase, and sampled frequencies and mixed channels must respect rotary dimension pairing. Test re-enhancement one period apart, not just tensor shapes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Convert seven days to 168 hours. Feeding the raw second count interprets the same interval as many incorrect periods.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26369">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.26369-clockrope/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-45fd047e4127727e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cmsl" data-paper-title="CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-cmsl-b229ccb6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-eff0ba3837f4f0a0">Why does CMSL condition contextual lenses on current nonsequence context?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acmsl">CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Context determines which historical events explain a latent intent together. Soft routing creates multiple strands for encoding and context-query aggregation, avoiding fixed business categories that hide more specific needs. Human-interpretable themes are not guaranteed; check redundancy and collapse.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Travel can emphasize light equipment, while a home context emphasizes storage within the same shopping history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28533">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.28533-cmsl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-eff0ba3837f4f0a0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cmsl" data-paper-title="CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-89f711951fa492ec">Why does CMSL&#x27;s contextual lens not prebucket events into click and purchase types?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acmsl">CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fixed event types need not match current latent intent. CMSL learns context-conditioned soft assignment into semantic strands, encodes them separately, and aggregates them using nonsequence context. Check duplication and loss of effective history rather than assuming strands are complementary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A kitchen-item click can indicate restocking or preparing to move. Different lenses can weight it differently without a fixed click bucket.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28533">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.28533-cmsl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-89f711951fa492ec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cmsl" data-paper-title="CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-829930983eb478a2">How do CMSL strands differ from simply adding attention heads?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acmsl">CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Heads project the same input sequence into different subspaces. A lens first reweights or groups events under context, creating distinct latent sequences before encoding. CMSL&#x27;s linear HSTU uses a specific kernel approximation; strands do not automatically linearize standard HSTU.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>More heads read the same ledger in different ways. Lenses first reorganize it into separate ledgers, which still need effective encoding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28533">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.28533-cmsl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-829930983eb478a2">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cmsl" data-paper-title="CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-cac1ed972c28ccb8">Why check width costs separately in CMSL&#x27;s second-order feature-map approximation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acmsl">CMSL: Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning for Recommendation Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Decomposing the SiLU dot product can reorder multiplication to reduce quadratic dependence on history length. Second-order cross terms grow with feature width, so linear length scaling does not settle FLOPs or constants. The local run checks learned lenses and an HSTU-style path; verify the production kernel separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Doubling history from 1,000 to 2,000 can roughly double the length term, while doubling feature width can expand the feature map by much more.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28533">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.28533-cmsl/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-cac1ed972c28ccb8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dcn-v2" data-paper-title="DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-dcn-v2-7ac56e9e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-31f19cb8fdc20457">Why does depth control the order of explicit crosses in DCN-V2?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adcn-v2">DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each layer elementwise multiplies a transform of current state by the original input, building higher orders while residuals retain lower ones. This gives traceable polynomial interaction paths, unlike generic MLP fitting. Rank, width, and training still constrain effective expressivity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A user age–category interaction can gain another original feature at the next layer without losing its lower-order residual.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2008.13535-dcn-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-31f19cb8fdc20457">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dcn-v2" data-paper-title="DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a5fba110bcfcd1e9">Why does each DCN-V2 cross layer multiply the current transform by the original input x₀?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adcn-v2">DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The original anchor creates traceable higher-order combinations as depth increases instead of relying solely on implicit MLP interactions. Matrix crosses increase expressivity; low-rank factors and expert gating control cost. Compression can reduce capacity and must be tested with the deep path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Cross user and category first, then multiply by the original time feature to form a third-order interaction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2008.13535-dcn-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a5fba110bcfcd1e9">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dcn-v2" data-paper-title="DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-46f4f5f89cf26086">What is the capacity-compute trade-off between DCN-V2 low-rank expert mixing and a full cross matrix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adcn-v2">DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>U and V factor the large matrix through a smaller subspace. Multiple gated experts add input-dependent flexibility but also storage and routing. A single low-rank expert limits representable directions; parameter savings do not imply equal end-to-end latency savings because embeddings and other modules still cost time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Project thousands of dimensions to dozens and back, with separate expert crosses. Too little rank can lose rare, important relationships.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2008.13535-dcn-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-46f4f5f89cf26086">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dcn-v2" data-paper-title="DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-80771f1fac3afa44">Which layers provide x0 and xl in DCN-V2?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adcn-v2">DCN V2: Improved Deep &amp; Cross Network and Practical Lessons for Web-scale Learning to Rank Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>x0 is always the cross stack&#x27;s original input and xl its current state; replacing x0 with xl changes the cross. Map each low-rank expert back to original width before multiplication and normalize gates over experts. Matching residual shapes does not verify the operator.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Layer two still multiplies the original user and item vectors rather than squaring the previous state, despite matching shapes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13535">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2008.13535-dcn-v2/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-80771f1fac3afa44">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:deepfm" data-paper-title="DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-deepfm-65a63b7d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-aa25bf5c7ee147c5">What do DeepFM&#x27;s first-order, second-order, and DNN outputs contribute?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adeepfm">DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>First-order terms give individual effects, FM vector products capture pairs, and the DNN learns richer nonlinear interactions. They meet in one click logit with shared embeddings; orders can overlap and probabilities should not be added.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A city effect, a city–category pair, and a more complex price/time condition all contribute to the same logit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04247">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1703.04247-deepfm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-aa25bf5c7ee147c5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:deepfm" data-paper-title="DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-c7aa48572635a536">Why do DeepFM&#x27;s FM and DNN share field embeddings?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adeepfm">DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>FM explicitly models first- and second-order terms and the DNN learns higher-order nonlinear interactions. Shared field semantics reduce duplicated parameters and manual crosses and let both paths train the embeddings. Their coupled gradients need not be conflict-free.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>FM learns occupation–category pairs, while DNN combines occupation, category, and price; both update the same field vectors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04247">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1703.04247-deepfm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c7aa48572635a536">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:deepfm" data-paper-title="DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-a20cf160a75d260a">How do DeepFM&#x27;s engineering assumptions differ from hand-crossed Wide &amp; Deep?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adeepfm">DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>FM learns pairwise relations from vector inner products and shares fields with the deep path, reducing manual crosses. Explicit crosses offer exact rules but cost coverage and maintenance. Embedding limits remain, as do field design and governance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>FM can learn city–category effects without one column per pair, but an illegal business combination still needs an explicit constraint.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04247">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1703.04247-deepfm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a20cf160a75d260a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:deepfm" data-paper-title="DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-41c1dda6c15dea15">Why sum only i&lt;j in DeepFM&#x27;s second-order term?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adeepfm">DeepFM: A Factorization-Machine based Neural Network for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei Noah&#x27;s Ark Lab</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>FM models distinct feature pairs. Self-products add squares and counting both orders changes scale. Efficient computation uses half the difference between the square of the sum and the sum of squares. The FM and DNN must share parameters, not copies with the same initial values.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Count age–category once, not age–age. Copies of vectors would diverge once the two paths train.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04247">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1703.04247-deepfm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-41c1dda6c15dea15">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dien" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-dien-3d6c73b7" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9c333f1e60e9ad6d">Why separate interest extraction and target-related evolution in DIEN?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adien">Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The first stage extracts predictive interest states from behavior with auxiliary supervision. The second uses candidate relevance to control their update strength for the target. This avoids equating raw clicks with interests and remains sensitive to auxiliary negatives and noisy histories.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Camera and lens views establish photography interest, which matters more for a travel camera than for a novel.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1809.03672-dien/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9c333f1e60e9ad6d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dien" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6b9b05c208996f59">How does DIEN multiplying target relevance into a GRU update gate differ from final history pooling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adien">Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Auxiliary prediction learns per-step interests, and candidate attention modulates each state update, letting relevant events revise memory while suppressing irrelevant changes. Late pooling cannot undo earlier overwrites. More recurrent computation need not help short histories.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For a lens recommendation, a random food-ad click should weakly update a strong photography state rather than overwrite it before final pooling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1809.03672-dien/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6b9b05c208996f59">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dien" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
