<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-50f77630c64f3a37">When does candidate information enter DIEN compared with DIN target attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adien">Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>DIN weights history at aggregation, whereas DIEN multiplies relevance into each recurrent update gate, controlling retained and new state throughout evolution. Extra computation and training are not guaranteed improvements; the local gain did not reproduce.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A lens view can revise recurrent state immediately for a camera candidate; late weighting only reads what survives existing compression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1809.03672-dien/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-50f77630c64f3a37">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dien" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fcaef89988ef9b8e">How should DIEN auxiliary next-event supervision avoid confusing training labels with test futures?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adien">Deep Interest Evolution Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Use next events as training labels while extraction inputs stop at current time and negatives follow training rules. Do not feed a held-out event into the GRU at evaluation. Target gating must update recurrent state step by step, not merely weight the final vector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Predict event three from position two during training; feeding event three when evaluating that prediction leaks the answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.03672">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1809.03672-dien/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fcaef89988ef9b8e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:din" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-din-dfe7b0eb" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c7ffdd9c88660a4">Why is DIN local interest candidate-conditioned rather than a single short-term interest?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adin">Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Local means the relevant subset of all history for the current target. A user can have several interests; candidate changes alter activations and aggregation without requiring one label. Attention cannot create missing evidence, and low activation does not imply permanent disinterest.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The same user can like science fiction and cooking, activating different histories for a movie and cookware.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1706.06978-din/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c7ffdd9c88660a4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:din" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-13240dbf0db3f265">Why can DIN produce different interest vectors for the same user?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adin">Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Which historical actions matter depends on the candidate. DIN learns activations from each candidate-action feature combination and pools accordingly. Greater expressivity prevents blanket reuse of the resulting state across candidates; compare against matched-budget pooling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Running socks emphasize running-shoe history, while baking tools emphasize oven activity in the same user history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1706.06978-din/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-13240dbf0db3f265">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:din" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-77536cb95e45f6d4">How does DIN local activation differ from dot-product attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adin">Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It takes the candidate, action, difference, and elementwise product to learn richer matching. Dice adapts its boundary to feature distributions. This does not imply causality or guaranteed gain; the local matched comparison showed no improvement over mean pooling.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Near-equal dot products can hide price differences and shared categories that the difference and product features highlight.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1706.06978-din/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-77536cb95e45f6d4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:din" data-paper-title="Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-fce6f5413a09b608">Over which axis should DIN normalize weights, and how should it handle padding?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adin">Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalize over valid history positions for one user and candidate, masking padding first. Do not normalize across candidates or batch examples. Keep Dice training statistics and serving state consistent without adjusting from test labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With three actions and five pads, distribute weights only over the three valid positions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1706.06978-din/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fce6f5413a09b608">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:echo-selector-loss" data-paper-title="ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-echo-selector-loss-59466a02" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-d7c77411b2cad8f3">Why retain history record addresses rather than only latent interest vectors in ECHO?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aecho-selector-loss">ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Latents are compact but cannot recover concrete candidate-specific events. Addressable records enable targeted small-subset retrieval and user-side reuse. This does not imply scanning all history per candidate; serving must follow the exported index and parameter path, beyond the local loss component.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A camera query can retrieve a recent macro-photography view and running shoes can retrieve exercise evidence, neither recoverable from a vague outdoors vector.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28569v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.28569-echo-selector-loss/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d7c77411b2cad8f3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:echo-selector-loss" data-paper-title="ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-1e00f3b69701b501">Why does ECHO distill the full teacher distribution and also penalize misses near the selection boundary?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aecho-selector-loss">ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Soft targets communicate relative history relevance but can leave crucial records outside a limited budget. Boundary pairs compare a better missed record against a weaker selected one, using detached teacher-score differences to drive swaps. The component retains addresses, and the local run verifies loss and gradients, not 100K-history performance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With budget two, the student misses a highly valued record and keeps a weak one. KD conveys overall order; the pair directly promotes the swap.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28569v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.28569-echo-selector-loss/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1e00f3b69701b501">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:echo-selector-loss" data-paper-title="ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f213f30adacee7d0">How do ECHO boundary pairs and full-distribution KD supervise different errors?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aecho-selector-loss">ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>KD transfers overall teacher preference; pairing missed strong records with selected weak ones focuses on swaps that change Top-K. Teacher quality gaps weight pairs. The discrete selection remains nondifferentiable; selected student logits receive gradients.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Positions ten and eleven can have similar global probabilities yet determine whether a vital record is kept. Boundary loss targets that pair.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28569v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.28569-echo-selector-loss/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f213f30adacee7d0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:echo-selector-loss" data-paper-title="ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-bb9a81762fca55db">Why normalize ECHO by valid pair weights across the batch and detach teacher values and weights?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aecho-selector-loss">ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Averaging by row can inflate requests with few pairs. Batch normalization preserves defined pair contributions. Freeze teacher and mining weights, update matching student scores only, and exclude padding from probabilities, selection, and gradients. A finite scalar alone is insufficient verification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>With ten pairs on one row and one on another, per-row means can give the lone pair tenfold relative weight; a shared denominator avoids that.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28569v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.28569-echo-selector-loss/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bb9a81762fca55db">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:fuxi-alpha" data-paper-title="FuXi-α: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-fuxi-alpha-d5540b18" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-bfdf2b6b061fc0a3">Why divide feature interactions across FuXi-α channels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afuxi-alpha">FuXi-α: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei / USTC</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Heterogeneous fields encode different relations; widening one space can still favor the strongest. Separate adaptive channels and staged FFN fusion can retain complementary structure, not guarantee it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Channels can specialize in user–item fit and context–price interaction, or all collapse to popularity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03036">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2502.03036-fuxi-alpha/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-bfdf2b6b061fc0a3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:fuxi-alpha" data-paper-title="FuXi-α: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-034c54f6610a2785">Why does FuXi-α use multiple interaction channels and staged FFNs instead of widening one attention path?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afuxi-alpha">FuXi-α: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei / USTC</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One path can mix unlike relationships in the same space. Adaptive channels model different interactions and multistage FFNs combine them gradually. Additional channels can still learn redundant patterns; compare single-channel and matched-budget configurations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>User–item, context–item, and history–candidate relations can be learned separately, but identical attention channels only add cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03036">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2502.03036-fuxi-alpha/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-034c54f6610a2785">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:fuxi-alpha" data-paper-title="FuXi-α: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-08ca36f70ea32158">Where does FuXi-α&#x27;s staged fusion differ from concatenating channel outputs only at the final head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afuxi-alpha">FuXi-α: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei / USTC</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Intermediate FFNs fuse current state and channel outputs before later layers, allowing further relation composition. Late fusion has one opportunity. Additional capacity costs more and did not prevent local NDCG decline.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A later layer can combine nighttime context and price sensitivity into demand for evening promotions rather than only merging final summaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03036">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2502.03036-fuxi-alpha/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-08ca36f70ea32158">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:fuxi-alpha" data-paper-title="FuXi-α: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-83eae398ef9dda36">What shapes and update order does FuXi-α require for progressive residual fusion?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Afuxi-alpha">FuXi-α: Scaling Recommendation Model with Feature Interaction Enhanced Transformer</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Huawei / USTC</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Channels may have distinct Q/K/V. Project their concatenated state back to backbone width for residual addition, preserve layer and old/new state order, and train channel weights rather than concatenate fixed similarities. Local comparisons only cover the implemented budget.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three d-wide channel outputs plus backbone features must pass through an FFN back to d before addition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03036">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2502.03036-fuxi-alpha/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-83eae398ef9dda36">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrank" data-paper-title="Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-genrank-a86f2304" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-c377e9c8c77101ce">Why can GenRank retain multi-action learning with items and actions at one position?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrank">Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Actions remain input features or supervision, just not separate positions. Position and time biases preserve temporal cues. This compresses organization, not behavioral relevance, and equivalence needs testing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An impression and its known click can share a position while clicks and skips remain different labels.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04180">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2505.04180-genrank/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c377e9c8c77101ce">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrank" data-paper-title="Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9b301295110c48a6">Why does merging actions into item tokens change HSTU-style ranking cost in GenRank?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrank">Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Interleaving doubles positions per event, increasing quadratic interactions. GenRank keeps action features or supervision on item positions and adds position/time biases. Fewer tokens do not guarantee equivalent expression; local quality changed alongside speed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Ten events become ten instead of twenty positions, reducing the attention matrix while potentially losing action dependencies.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04180">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2505.04180-genrank/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9b301295110c48a6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrank" data-paper-title="Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-0c454283f597f484">Why compare latency and AUC for GenRank versus interleaved item/action ranking?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrank">Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fewer positions reduce attention work but can sacrifice interaction expressivity. Local latency and AUC both decreased, so efficiency is not unchanged accuracy or superiority to HSTU. Hardware and candidates limit extrapolation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One hundred events can use 100 rather than 200 positions but lose action-order detail; speed alone hides that.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04180">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2505.04180-genrank/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0c454283f597f484">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrank" data-paper-title="Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-4dcd00e7785d310d">Why not input GenRank&#x27;s current prediction target like historical actions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrank">Towards Large-scale Generative Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>History actions are known and can accompany items; the current action is the label. Separate fields and causal masks and use only request-time information in position/time bias. Matching shapes do not rule out leakage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Include a prior camera click, not the true future click on the shoe being scored.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04180">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2505.04180-genrank/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4dcd00e7785d310d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrec-netflix" data-paper-title="GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-genrec-netflix-691b65fa" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-443e09eaf7bff5ef">How does Netflix GenRec&#x27;s catalog-aware head prevent out-of-catalog hallucinations?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrec-netflix">GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Netflix</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A pooled prefill state scores only fixed catalog item IDs, not generated names. Text context and a language objective supply semantics. In-catalog outputs can still be irrelevant or unavailable; inventory and serving mappings need separate checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An unreleased title known to the LLM cannot be recommended if there is no output column for it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10257">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.10257-genrec-netflix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-443e09eaf7bff5ef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrec-netflix" data-paper-title="GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-7c9e2f93989e3d7b">Why does Netflix GenRec not generate a recommendation list token by token despite using a decoder-only LLM?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrec-netflix">GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Netflix</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One prefill encodes text context, then a catalog-aware head scores items directly. This keeps semantic interactions while avoiding multi-step decoding and out-of-catalog generation. A joint language objective improves representation, not free-form serving; the local single seed does not establish Netflix-scale gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Score every catalog movie once instead of writing one title and feeding it back to generate the next.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10257">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.10257-genrec-netflix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7c9e2f93989e3d7b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrec-netflix" data-paper-title="GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-da9c9def46906001">How does Netflix GenRec reward-weighted ranking differ from online RL over generated lists?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrec-netflix">GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Netflix</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multiple rewards weight examples in supervised catalog ranking, alongside a language objective. There is no token-by-token rollout or list policy gradient; serving uses prefill scoring. The two reward uses have different probability and compute paths.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Giving a satisfied example more loss weight is not generating ten online results and running PPO.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10257">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.10257-genrec-netflix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-da9c9def46906001">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:genrec-netflix" data-paper-title="GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-6926175c877ccaf4">Why isn&#x27;t Netflix GenRec&#x27;s local GRU comparison a parameter-matched architecture ablation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Agenrec-netflix">GenRec: An LLM-Backed Recommendation Ranker at Netflix</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Netflix</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The experiment loads a larger public causal LLM and trains LoRA, while the baseline is ID-only GRU. Parameters and semantic inputs differ; it compares pipelines, not one isolated operator. Single seed, reduced catalog, and proxy rewards also preclude comparing directly to reported online percentages.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>LLM gains may come from title semantics or pretrained weights, not entirely from the catalog head.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 本地复现, 对照口径. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10257">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2608.10257-genrec-netflix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6926175c877ccaf4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ha-moe" data-paper-title="Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-ha-moe-beffade8" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4d9f4d295ac21e2b">Why choose HA-MoE experts by heterogeneity instead of one fixed model per content type?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aha-moe">Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google / Discover</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent models cannot share common knowledge, while one tower can favor high-volume content. Gated combinations share useful general signals while retaining specialization, which must be measured rather than assumed from expert names.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Sports news can use both a freshness expert and a sports specialist.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27577">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.27577-ha-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4d9f4d295ac21e2b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ha-moe" data-paper-title="Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-dda89f7194e99a78">Why route HA-MoE experts by content heterogeneity and monitor domain DL-AUC?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aha-moe">Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google / Discover</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>In mixed feeds, frequent domains can dominate shared gradients. Contextual gates combine general and specialist experts, and per-domain metrics plus utilization reveal degradation masked by averages. More experts do not prove specialization.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>News volume can hide sports-video losses in aggregate scores, which domain monitoring exposes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27577">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.27577-ha-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dda89f7194e99a78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ha-moe" data-paper-title="Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-2e44383e9cb5eef1">Why can LENS per-domain DL-AUC disagree with aggregate AUC?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aha-moe">Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google / Discover</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>High-volume domains dominate aggregates. Slice metrics and expert usage show which types are ignored and where gains originate. Monitoring does not guarantee learning; local NDCG did not rise, and lower head share is not a quality substitute.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If video is 90% of traffic, a slight video gain can mask a large news regression.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27577">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.27577-ha-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2e44383e9cb5eef1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:ha-moe" data-paper-title="Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-82c0025bf2b8bc76">Over what axis should HA-MoE apply gate softmax, and what should LENS group by?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aha-moe">Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google / Discover</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Normalize per example over experts and align expert outputs before mixing. Record utilization by domain and time. Local session entropy proxies heterogeneity and measures a fixed expert set, not all open-web content.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Give one news request weights over four experts; do not normalize news and video examples together.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27577">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.27577-ha-moe/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-82c0025bf2b8bc76">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:helix" data-paper-title="HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-helix-94ed43e6" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-21fa62a2c298c656">Why does HELIX expand both sequence modeling and heterogeneous feature interaction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahelix">HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>History and feature combinations supply distinct information. Interleaved modules let candidate states read history at multiple depths while preserving user-only state. This is not late concatenation, and caching constrains direction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Layers can combine travel history with price and device features; enlarging either path alone cannot provide the other&#x27;s evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37183">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.37183-helix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-21fa62a2c298c656">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:helix" data-paper-title="HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fdc7e424eea56b8a">Why does HELIX forbid candidate tokens from writing back to shared sequence state?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahelix">HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>One-way dependence keeps expensive user-history encoding candidate-independent and reusable within a request while candidates repeatedly read it for deep interaction. Writes back would make history candidate-dependent. Local checks cover sensitivity and cache invariance, not production throughput or gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A shoe can reuse the history read by a camera only if the camera did not modify that state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37183">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.37183-helix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fdc7e424eea56b8a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:helix" data-paper-title="HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-63277b17cffa622f">How do HELIX one-way communication and WHALE-style bidirectional exchange differ in cacheability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahelix">HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>HELIX blocks candidate-conditioned writes into public sequence state. Bidirectional exchange allows deeper co-evolution but creates candidate dependence. Both can use cross-attention without equivalent dependencies, and no universal quality ordering follows.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>After a camera reads shared history, shoes can read the same cache only if the camera state never wrote back.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37183">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.37183-helix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-63277b17cffa622f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:helix" data-paper-title="HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-d081140a6218cc83">Why check candidate deltas, invariant user caches, and finite gradients in HELIX?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahelix">HELIX: Purified and Unified - Rethinking Feature Interaction and Sequence Modeling for Large-Scale Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · TikTok / ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Candidate changes should alter scores without changing public user state. Missing either indicates ignored candidates or cache pollution; finite loss and gradients test trainability. These are diagnostics, not quality metrics.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Identical scores suggest candidate insensitivity; changing scores and cache together breaks sharing despite successful forward execution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37183">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.37183-helix/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d081140a6218cc83">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hisac" data-paper-title="HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-hisac-bc7a3c37" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5cf60ed6519d3925">Why aren&#x27;t HiSAC interest agents a group of live language agents?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahisac">HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Taobao</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each is a representation aggregated from hierarchical codes and behavior. Quantization, voting, routing, and weighting operate over related nodes without independent LLM calls. The name describes structure, not agent reasoning or serving cost.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Photography and camping agents can be two vectors; selecting one needs no inter-agent messages or generated text.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21009">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.21009-hisac/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5cf60ed6519d3925">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hisac" data-paper-title="HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-4e26b8af5e5c89d6">Why does HiSAC form hierarchical interest agents and route each query to only a few?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahisac">HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Taobao</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Full-history attention is expensive and one summary can lose long-tail interests. Hierarchical codes and voting create personalized compressed units; queries read only relevant ones. These are not autonomous LLMs, and routing cannot recover interests lost in compression or assignment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>For lenses, read the photography agent rather than cooking or cycling; discarded astrophotography evidence remains unavailable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21009">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.21009-hisac/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4e26b8af5e5c89d6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hisac" data-paper-title="HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-73ff7709cf627e84">What choices does HiSAC&#x27;s hierarchical interest routing retain compared with a single fixed user vector?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahisac">HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Taobao</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Separate nodes preserve interests at different levels of granularity, and a query can use them as needed instead of averaging away multiple modes. A single vector gives a simpler interface but makes individual sub-interests harder to recover. Routing may miss rare, low-weight needs, and quantization can lose detail. The source&#x27;s small NDCG increase and Hit decrease should be interpreted separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A camera query can read the photography node for a user who likes photography and running, while running shoes can read the sports node. Averaging the two interests into one vector may dilute both.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21009">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.21009-hisac/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-73ff7709cf627e84">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hisac" data-paper-title="HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-b820ba3ed40479e1">Why must HiSAC explicitly handle empty nodes and repeated votes when aggregating behavior by code?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahisac">HiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba / Taobao</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The node mean is normalized by total valid weight. An empty node provides no evidence of an interest and must not produce a strong signal. Hierarchical votes and query-selected subsets must preserve identity. Repeated behavior should count as defined, but expanding one event across levels must not turn it into several independent consumption events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: One photography event can populate both a coarse and a fine node without implying two purchases. An empty diving node is not a real interest just because its initial vector happens to look similar.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21009">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2602.21009-hisac/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b820ba3ed40479e1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hpgr" data-paper-title="Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-hpgr-f17a7799" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-61bf64fdb6e80c78">Why does HPGR use masked session modeling to learn a behavioral hierarchy?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahpgr">Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harbin Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Events in a session often share intent, while a change of session may reflect a shift in intent. Learning both levels gives the later preference selector a more meaningful state. A flat sequence based on adjacent positions can mix separate visits. Pretraining supervision comes from observed training data; test input must not reveal a target that should be unknown.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: One visit focuses on tents and sleeping bags, the next on hiking boots. A session encoder can distinguish the two needs rather than treating every item as part of one continuous intent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00980">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2603.00980-hpgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-61bf64fdb6e80c78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hpgr" data-paper-title="Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-f5ebe6d332af25ec">Why does HPGR use masked session pretraining before selecting history with preference-guided sparse attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahpgr">Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harbin Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Session structure captures relationships within a stretch of behavior. Learning it with masking avoids treating the entire long history as a flat sequence of interchangeable events. At fine-tuning time, the current preference selects related history so computation focuses on useful evidence rather than just cutting by recency. Sparse selection can still miss rare but decisive interests, so check selection coverage along with final predictions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Last week&#x27;s camera comparisons belong to one session and can be retrieved together for today&#x27;s lens candidate. The latest unrelated purchase should not displace that organized history just because it is newer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00980">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2603.00980-hpgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f5ebe6d332af25ec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hpgr" data-paper-title="Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7cfc34a2cc8db770">What older evidence can HPGR use that a fixed recent window might miss?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahpgr">Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harbin Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A recent window retains events by time. Preference-guided sparse selection picks events for the current intent, letting older relevant history compete for a limited budget. It depends on the selector: downstream layers cannot read omitted events, and hierarchical pretraining does not guarantee correct selection. The public proxy gains in the source apply only to its protocol.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: If the latest browsing was for novels but the current candidate is a camera, the selector may find older photography history that the last ten events omit. A bad selector could also revive an outdated interest.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00980">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2603.00980-hpgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7cfc34a2cc8db770">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hpgr" data-paper-title="Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-0a1842453e297052">How should HPGR keep padding and future targets out of its top-k attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahpgr">Beyond the Flat Sequence: Hierarchical and Preference-Aware Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Harbin Institute of Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Score only eligible historical events, mask padding before top-k, and enforce the current-time cutoff. If there are fewer than k events, use the valid count instead of duplicating dummy records. Align session boundaries with the preference query; do not use the gold next item to create a condition unavailable at test time.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: With three valid events and k=5, attention can read only those three. Unmasked zero-scored padding can beat real events with negative scores.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00980">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2603.00980-hpgr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0a1842453e297052">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-hstu-2703dd1e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d826e4c63d0f978">Do HSTU history tokens interact, unlike a static history vector?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Yes. Each position updates by reading visible earlier tokens, producing contextual history that a target later reads. Causality restricts direction, not history interaction; outside-window events remain absent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A lens event can incorporate earlier camera context before a tripod candidate reads it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d826e4c63d0f978">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-defbb4068319dd08">Why do ranking and retrieval predict different objects in HSTU?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retrieval predicts a relevant next item. Ranking conditions on the candidate to predict actions, interleaving item/action tokens. Full-catalog next-item metrics do not validate every action task.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Guess a film versus predict clicks or long watch for an already given film.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-defbb4068319dd08">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d1b7f594100aaa20">Why remove softmax but normalize after aggregation and apply a U gate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Softmax fixes weight mass and can suppress behavior-frequency intensity. Pointwise SiLU aggregation preserves variation; post-normalization stabilizes and the token-conditioned U gate modulates output. Causal window interactions are not linear complexity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>One versus ten related events can differ before the gate controls how much information passes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2402.17152-hstu/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d1b7f594100aaa20">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:hstu" data-paper-title="Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-3b88d0c3b149bbc6">Why not interpret local matched-budget SASRec losses as industrial superiority?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Ahstu">Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Matched width, layers, loss, and steps isolate a local core. MovieLens lacks heterogeneous events, timing, long histories, and scale. Preserve local negatives without dismissing paper production evidence or importing it.</p>
