</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-a18a983529fe37d7">How do independent FFNs learn interactions after fixed TokenMix?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Split every input by head and concatenate matching-index slices into new tokens, so specialized nonlinear FFNs receive cross-field signals. H=T and divisible width are layout conditions. Field mixing does not forbid sequence attention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>User, product, and context slices can jointly enter an FFN without similarity weights.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a18a983529fe37d7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-473b102f64b8ecd6">What do ReLU routing and DTSI solve beyond fixed top-k?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sparse ReLU permits variable activated experts. Separate training and inference routers apply sparsity only on inference so experts can learn without starvation. Local sparse code does not validate full dual routing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Complex tokens can use more experts while rarely deployed experts still train.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-473b102f64b8ecd6">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-603d4772b072a0eb">Why not credit TokenMix alone for the dense versus shared-FFN gain?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Both arms use TokenMix; dedicated versus shared FFNs and different parameter counts change together. The sparse arm also trails dense. Report budgets and popularity bias; local results do not establish paper MFU or A/B.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Both cars already use the same transmission, so a larger engine&#x27;s gain does not isolate it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-603d4772b072a0eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-67c000ac06ff074b">Why require H=T and divisible hidden dimension?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Splitting T tokens of width D into H slices gives H outputs of width TD/H. H=T restores T×D for residual addition; D must divide by H.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four 64-wide tokens split into four 16-wide slices; three heads cannot split 64 evenly.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-67c000ac06ff074b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankmixer" data-paper-title="RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ad1e554a4b682966">Do RankMixer per-token FFNs attach to original fields or mixed positions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankmixer">RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Each FFN sees a mixed token containing same-index slices from all fields. Its parameters specialize in that subspace, not one original field. Preserve field/head/output layout.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The first mixed FFN processes parts of all four fields, not only the first one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15551">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15551-rankmixer/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ad1e554a4b682966">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankup" data-paper-title="RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-rankup-a9399758" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-94f1626a3266cd89">Why isn&#x27;t higher RankUp representation rank proof of useful interests?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankup">RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Rank measures independent directions, not task information. Noise can raise rank and obscure useful structure. Inspect spectra with task and subgroup metrics rather than claiming quality when tokens become less alike.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Random orthogonal user noise can yield full rank without adding any predictive preference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2604.17878-rankup/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-94f1626a3266cd89">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankup" data-paper-title="RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-0478859fae50a11a">Why use permutation grouping and global tokens against RankUp rank collapse instead of merely adding embeddings or depth?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankup">RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Added parameters can reuse the same subspace. Different groupings and tables alter interaction paths, global tokens connect groups, and external features and task decoupling add signals. These aim to turn capacity into richer directions, not guarantee effective rank.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: New groupings let fields interact that never shared a group under a fixed partition.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2604.17878-rankup/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-0478859fae50a11a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankup" data-paper-title="RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-f98e38ec565ff9d5">How does permutation grouping change interaction opportunities versus fully shared RankUp input?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankup">RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>New partitions let previously separated fields meet, independent embeddings add views, and global tokens connect groups. Shared inputs can favor strong fields, while groups can miss or duplicate crosses. Combined local changes do not attribute gains to one component.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Another permutation can put age with category; unaligned parameter shuffling can instead destroy meaning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2604.17878-rankup/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f98e38ec565ff9d5">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rankup" data-paper-title="RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-075dc39c4c00dc0e">Why track RankUp permutation matrices and field identities together?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arankup">RankUp: Towards High-rank Representations for Large Scale Advertising Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Tencent</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>XP rearranges inputs; corresponding embedding and group weights must follow the same map. Align global-token residual widths, and do not choose permutations using test labels. A local proxy does not verify production scaling laws.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Swapping price and age while keeping the original lookup can interpret age 18 as a price.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17878">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2604.17878-rankup/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-075dc39c4c00dc0e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:recap-ctr" data-paper-title="Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-recap-ctr-8a9efe0a" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-5aaae777d05508db">Is averaging RECAP-CTR route logits equivalent to averaging click probabilities?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arecap-ctr">Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Sigmoid is nonlinear. The source averages logits first, which does not turn shared routes into independent complete models.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: With logits 0 and 4, sigmoid of their mean is about 0.88; mean sigmoid is about 0.74.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37905">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.37905-recap-ctr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5aaae777d05508db">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:recap-ctr" data-paper-title="Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-6d48a3ea0b094184">Why share recursive blocks in RECAP-CTR yet average routes and retain a training-trajectory EMA?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arecap-ctr">Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different routes through shared blocks produce multiple logits without independent models. Averaging reduces route fluctuations; EMA smooths weights over training time. Correlated routes limit benefit. Local evidence verifies state and operator invariants only.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Two recursive routes yield slightly different click scores; average those while separately smoothing neighboring training checkpoints.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37905">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.37905-recap-ctr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-6d48a3ea0b094184">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:recap-ctr" data-paper-title="Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e72f1a396b8fee34">Why can&#x27;t route averaging replace trajectory EMA in RECAP-CTR?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arecap-ctr">Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Route averaging combines simultaneous outputs; EMA smooths parameters over time. Shared routes can remain correlated and EMA can lag drift. Local invariants do not show CTR lift from smoothing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: All routes can share a high bias, and EMA can smooth an unusual step without adding a missing feature.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37905">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.37905-recap-ctr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e72f1a396b8fee34">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:recap-ctr" data-paper-title="Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ec50d7a4585aae79">Why checkpoint RECAP-CTR EMA state separately?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arecap-ctr">Beyond Interaction Capacity: Estimator Scaling with Recursive Models for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Georgia Institute of Technology / Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>EMA accumulates parameter history across steps, so losing it changes the estimator on resume. Match route count and averaging denominator rather than treating missing routes as zero. Verify recurrence, EMA updates, and export separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Resetting EMA to current parameters after interruption loses thousands of smoothed steps even if training resumes.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37905">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.37905-recap-ctr/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ec50d7a4585aae79">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:repair-state" data-paper-title="Not All Is Lost: Repairing Lossy User Preference States of Personalization Encoders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-repair-state-eec04848" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-834d6a05b8e38552">Why aren&#x27;t a historical ht and current preference z interchangeable?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arepair-state">Not All Is Lost: Repairing Lossy User Preference States of Personalization Encoders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>ht represents a contextual position and z summarizes current preference for the head. Equal dimensions do not imply the same time or coverage. Repair selects evidence while retaining current state rather than replacing it wholesale.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Last year&#x27;s camera state cannot replace a current profile that includes camping.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01270">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.01270-repair-state/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-834d6a05b8e38552">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:repair-state" data-paper-title="Not All Is Lost: Repairing Lossy User Preference States of Personalization Encoders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-d799684e7cf1cfcc">Why repair preference with cached state differences while freezing Repair-State&#x27;s encoder and head?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arepair-state">Not All Is Lost: Repairing Lossy User Preference States of Personalization Encoders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Cached states retain evidence at different times. Select long-range, recent, or burst segments and add weighted differences to restore compressed directions without retraining. It cannot recover uncached evidence and can reintroduce stale interests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Retrieve recent baby-product activity from cache to supplement a profile dominated by long-term movie viewing.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01270">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.01270-repair-state/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d799684e7cf1cfcc">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:repair-state" data-paper-title="Not All Is Lost: Repairing Lossy User Preference States of Personalization Encoders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-7595444adbde5955">How does Repair-State differ from retraining the encoder?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arepair-state">Not All Is Lost: Repairing Lossy User Preference States of Personalization Encoders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Postprocessing uses an existing forward cache while preserving encoder and head, reducing deployment cost. Retraining can change feature extraction. Residuals cannot recreate omitted evidence, and selection may not transfer to all tasks. The local diagnostic does not establish capability rankings.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: A stored burst can be restored, but an event ignored entirely by the encoder cannot.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01270">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.01270-repair-state/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7595444adbde5955">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:repair-state" data-paper-title="Not All Is Lost: Repairing Lossy User Preference States of Personalization Encoders" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-21fc126e36070136">Why check valid history before Repair-State top-k and masked softmax?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arepair-state">Not All Is Lost: Repairing Lossy User Preference States of Personalization Encoders</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · 原文首页未列第一作者机构</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Mask padding, future states, and other users before selection and normalize only selected valid states. Align differences with z. Define empty-history fallback rather than injecting random evidence. Frozen encoders do not prevent data leakage.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: With two events and k=5, zero-scored padding must not beat valid negative scores and pull z toward zero.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01270">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.01270-repair-state/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-21fc126e36070136">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rest" data-paper-title="From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-rest-5ed56a69" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-587482482f0ab50e">Why combine RoPE and relative time in ReST?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arest">From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position and elapsed time differ: adjacent events can be a minute or a year apart. RoPE represents order, time encoding adds cadence, and dual gates filter noise. Not all periodicity is captured and large gaps are not always irrelevant.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Camera views five minutes apart suggest one comparison; views six months apart may mark a new need.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01240">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.01240-rest/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-587482482f0ab50e">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rest" data-paper-title="From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ffc3ae495ed6b99c">Why separate heavy user encoding and light candidate interaction in ReST compute-once, decode-many?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arest">From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Long-history gated attention, order, and time intervals are shared user compute. Candidate cross-decoders read relevant evidence without rerunning history. Dual gates suppress noise, but only candidate-independent state is reusable and history/version changes invalidate it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Encode history once for 200 films, then let each query it; never share one film&#x27;s interaction result as general user state.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01240">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.01240-rest/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ffc3ae495ed6b99c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rest" data-paper-title="From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b147c7ec89040e41">What evidence does ReST gating preserve compared with truncation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arest">From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Truncation discards events; gating can suppress noise across broader history while retaining distant evidence for candidate decoding. It can suppress important items too and still incurs input cost. A small local regression does not show gating beats recent-window baselines.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: Keep a small weight on old photography and downweight accidental news; truncation could remove the useful photography event entirely.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01240">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.01240-rest/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b147c7ec89040e41">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:rest" data-paper-title="From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-106636ac34f6a61f">What dependencies matter before reusing ReST encoder caches across requests?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Arest">From Language to Behavior: Scaling Sequence Transformers for Industrial Recommendation Ranking with Rec-Native Designs</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Same-request hU reuse requires unchanged history and version. New events, relative time encodings, or model updates can invalidate cross-request state. Candidate decoder outputs remain private to their candidates. Local structure does not prove production QPS or cache lifecycle.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Illustration: After a user buys a camera, update history instead of reusing the old summary forever because user ID matches.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01240">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.01240-rest/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-106636ac34f6a61f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sam" data-paper-title="Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">

<span id="paper-recommendation-sam-b9df9dfc" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-f667ebf89a92beef">Does SAM blacklist same-category items after a purchase?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asam">Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It softly suppresses attention to related history and restores it over time, not permanent candidate filtering. Other evidence can still support recommendations.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Buying shampoo reduces old browsing influence without banning hair products.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.12714-sam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-f667ebf89a92beef">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sam" data-paper-title="Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-90747e26d9c7c6ae">Why suppress related history after buying and restore it near replenishment?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asam">Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>A purchase can complete an intent. Find its related history and estimate personal rhythm; time gates and log masks suppress then restore it. Completion is not dislike. Local ratings proxy purchases, not actual replenishment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Reduce detergent repeats immediately, then restore after likely use rather than suppress forever.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.12714-sam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-90747e26d9c7c6ae">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sam" data-paper-title="Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-c312c786eab5bae1">How does SAM differ from a fixed post-purchase cooldown?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asam">Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>It personalizes suppression by history and long-term purchase rhythm. Errors can still hurt, and nonreplenishable products may not fit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Coffee and televisions should not share a one-week rule.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.12714-sam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c312c786eab5bae1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sam" data-paper-title="Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2bd429203c7ebdc1">Where is SAM&#x27;s mask applied, and what are the local limits?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asam">Learning to Forget: Satiation-Aware Long-Sequence Transducers for Mitigating Post-Purchase Redundancy</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba Group</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Add a positive log mask to attention logits with numeric safeguards, not a multiplier on final scores. No real replenishment or censored purchase logs; only mechanisms and failure boundaries.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Guard near-zero masks without claiming accurate repurchase cycles.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.12714-sam/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2bd429203c7ebdc1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sasrec" data-paper-title="Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-sasrec-6f67bc6e" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-7d35ae6cc7ed04c8">How does SASRec shift inputs and next-item targets?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asasrec">Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Position i reads history through i and supervises the following item, without exposing future events. Exclude padding; each sequence yields several prefix tasks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use A→B and A,B→C; the representation predicting B cannot read C.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1808.09781-sasrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7d35ae6cc7ed04c8">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sasrec" data-paper-title="Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-9e5caa204add37ff">How does SASRec balance recent and distant interests without reading future?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asasrec">Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Content attention accesses several earlier behaviors beyond fixed-order Markov neighbors, without RNN recurrence. Position representations preserve order and causal masks restrict reads. Next item is supervision only, and attention can still read irrelevant history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Recall old sci-fi interest despite recent comedy, while position three cannot read item four.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1808.09781-sasrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9e5caa204add37ff">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sasrec" data-paper-title="Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-128c509fca314590">How does causal next-item prediction differ from masked item recovery?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asasrec">Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Causal training uses only history; masked recovery can use both neighbors. Right context legal for recovery is future leakage in next-item prediction.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Recovering A,[MASK],C may read C; predicting B after only A may not.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/1808.09781-sasrec/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-128c509fca314590">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sasrec" data-paper-title="Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7b580fbe795a484e">How preserve SASRec embeddings and negative objective?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asasrec">Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · UC San Diego</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Tie input item embeddings with output weights and use per-position positive and sampled-negative pairwise BCE, not catalog CE. Mask padding and future positions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Never sample the true positive as its own negative.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:semantic-native-longseq" data-paper-title="Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-semantic-native-longseq-dee361e1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-707a5bb5919e2395">Does a shared Semantic-Native SID prefix mean identical videos?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asemantic-native-longseq">Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Prefixes encode coarse similarity; identity still depends on the complete path and catalog mapping. Semantic sharing does not merge interaction records.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Distinct camping videos can share a prefix but keep different logs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07546">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.07546-semantic-native-longseq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-707a5bb5919e2395">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:semantic-native-longseq" data-paper-title="Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-63e5da9e21228955">Why compress both SID vocabulary and temporal sequence?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asemantic-native-longseq">Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Atomic ID tables grow with inventory, and full attention grows quadratically. Bounded hierarchical SID handles representation size; event folding reduces time positions and global queries gather interests. Both sacrifice detail.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Fold 48 events into 12 local tokens and share semantic codes, but do not assume original within-window order survives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07546">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.07546-semantic-native-longseq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-63e5da9e21228955">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:semantic-native-longseq" data-paper-title="Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8b1c2fa9a1b3c3ca">How does temporal folding differ from retaining only recent history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asemantic-native-longseq">Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Folding combines neighboring events into features and keeps coarse older information; truncation drops it. Folding and global queries do not preserve full temporal resolution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Four events compressed into one token can lose ordering without discarding all evidence.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07546">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.07546-semantic-native-longseq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8b1c2fa9a1b3c3ca">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:semantic-native-longseq" data-paper-title="Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence Modeling" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-7ff6d57f3d2e041c">Does the local folding exactly match paper channel rearrangement?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asemantic-native-longseq">Beyond Item IDs: Scaling Short-Form-Video Recommendation via Semantic-Native Long Sequence Modeling</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. Mean/recent is a proxy; no Google RQ-VAE or production components. Pool always-valid global queries and exclude padding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Mean folding tests coarse compression, not the paper tensor layout.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07546">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2606.07546-semantic-native-longseq/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-7ff6d57f3d2e041c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sequenceo1" data-paper-title="SequenceO1: End-to-End Ultra-Long (100K) Sequence Modeling in Recommendation with Low-Rank Caching" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-sequenceo1-53b97674" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-9ce0f15f4b39cfbb">Is a SequenceO1 sketch original distant history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asequenceo1">SequenceO1: End-to-End Ultra-Long (100K) Sequence Modeling in Recommendation with Low-Rank Caching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. A fixed-budget prototype representation summarizes remote behavior while recent history remains finer. It is not event-by-event recoverable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Thousands of events can form a few prototypes without preserving exact times.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08443">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.08443-sequenceo1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-9ce0f15f4b39cfbb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sequenceo1" data-paper-title="SequenceO1: End-to-End Ultra-Long (100K) Sequence Modeling in Recommendation with Low-Rank Caching" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-8c0f466df9e7082f">What does a fixed remote sketch bound, and what still scales?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asequenceo1">SequenceO1: End-to-End Ultra-Long (100K) Sequence Modeling in Recommendation with Low-Rank Caching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Candidate–sketch matching uses fixed prototypes; recent behavior remains detailed and STCA connects timescales. Reading, building, and updating the sketch still cost work. The local proxy is not the industrial path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Matching dozens of prototypes is bounded, but constructing them from 100,000 events is not free.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08443">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.08443-sequenceo1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8c0f466df9e7082f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sequenceo1" data-paper-title="SequenceO1: End-to-End Ultra-Long (100K) Sequence Modeling in Recommendation with Low-Rank Caching" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-d39fd3f417fbc390">How does sketch plus recent differ from recent-only truncation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asequenceo1">SequenceO1: End-to-End Ultra-Long (100K) Sequence Modeling in Recommendation with Low-Rank Caching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Sketch preserves compressed long-term patterns, whereas truncation drops remote history. Prototypes can still merge different interests.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>An older sports preference can survive a temporary travel streak.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08443">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.08443-sequenceo1/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-d39fd3f417fbc390">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sequenceo1" data-paper-title="SequenceO1: End-to-End Ultra-Long (100K) Sequence Modeling in Recommendation with Low-Rank Caching" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">

<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ede261f2274aee28">Is the local 0.65/0.35 blend the paper&#x27;s 100K-history formula?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asequenceo1">SequenceO1: End-to-End Ultra-Long (100K) Sequence Modeling in Recommendation with Low-Rank Caching</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · ByteDance / Douyin</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>No. It is a public scoring proxy; no production STCA or long-history service. Fix normalization and candidate masks and do not tune blend on test.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Small-catalog score gains do not show end-to-end latency with 100,000 events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>

<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sim" data-paper-title="Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-sim-df73a28d" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-3e6a146e9f258a78">Why run GSU search before ESU attention?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asim">Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Lifelong histories are long. Cheap candidate-related retrieval narrows them before fine matching, rather than always taking recent events.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A camera candidate can retrieve older photography behavior.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2006.05639-sim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3e6a146e9f258a78">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sim" data-paper-title="Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ff2b1a817c0aa800">Why use GSU then ESU instead of scoring lifelong history directly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asim">Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Most history is irrelevant per candidate. Cheap GSU narrows it, then ESU attends precisely to selected behavior. Fine matching cannot recover evidence omitted by coarse retrieval.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If category filtering excludes old lens interactions, later camera attention cannot see them.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2006.05639-sim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ff2b1a817c0aa800">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sim" data-paper-title="Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-e023b625f1151b67">How does candidate-related selection differ from one user vector?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asim">Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Different candidates retrieve different evidence. A shared user vector compresses once and is easy to cache. Quality and cost still need measurement.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Shoes and books can activate different historical interests for one user.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05639">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2006.05639-sim/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-e023b625f1151b67">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:sim" data-paper-title="Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/history-ranking-backbones">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / User histories and ranking backbones</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-24ca72f5435a3fec">How prevent future leakage in SIM top-k history?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Asim">Search-based User Interest Modeling with Lifelong Sequential Behavior Data for CTR Prediction</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Alibaba</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>GSU searches only pre-request history, separate from the target label. ESU sees selected entries only. MovieLens verifies mechanism, not production or online A/B.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Do not add the next actual click before searching history.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
